children: As cash-strapped consumers dine out less, McDonald's needs to show that it can use its enormous scale to get more people to visit its restaurants again. It intends to do just that with McDonald's > NEXT-a strategy that's designed to bring in more customers more often and help franchisees become more profitable.

At its investor day on Wednesday, McDonald's laid out a series of long-term financial targets tied to its NEXT strategy, which was unveiled in June. The plan focuses on improving menu items, using customer data and digital tools to make marketing more targeted, modernizing restaurants with AI and automation, simplifying operations, and giving employees better tools and training to improve service.

To help franchisees speed up these changes, McDonald's said it plans to spend about $8.5 billion on NEXT through 2036-through a mix of rent relief and capital assistance-starting with an initial push of $5 billion through 2030.

From 2027 to 2030, the fast-food gaint expects to spend about $3 billion a year on baseline capital expenditures, plus another $1.5 billion to $2 billion in cumulative capital to help its partners accelerate the rollout of NEXT. That brings the average annual spending to a range of $3.4 billion to $3.5 billion.
McDonald's had previously expected 2027 capital spending to rise by $300 million to $500 million from the $3.7 billion to $3.9 billion planned for 2026.
Investors have shown some initial reservation about the new spending plan. McDonald's shares fell 6% in Wednesday trading. The benchmark S&P 500 index slipped 0.7%.

McDonald's said the investment will pay back. As the NEXT elements are deployed throughout its U.S. and international stores, it expects gross restaurant-level efficiency to improve 2.5 percentage points. The company forecasts an operating margin in the low-to-mid 50% range by 2030, up from 47% in the first half of 2026.

The company expects new restaurants to add about 2.5 percentage points to systemwide sales growth in 2027, which would moderate to 2 percentage points by 2030. That would bring general and administrative expenses to about 1.9% of systemwide sales by 2030, down from 2.2% expected for 2026. The company's previous plan called for 4% to 5% annual net new restaurant growth and aimed to have 50,000 restaurants globally by the end of 2027.

"McDonald's scale and financial strength reflects decades of disciplined execution, prudent decision-making, and a proven ability to create long-term value," Chief Financial Officer Ian Borden said in a statement. "The financial targets we are introducing today are grounded in the expected economics of Restaurant > NEXT and the opportunities we see ahead."

The update comes at an important moment for the fast-food industry. Lower-income consumers remain strained by persistently high costs for everyday necessities, while restaurant operators are contending with elevated labor and ingredient expenses.

On August 4, McDonald's reported second-quarter revenue that was 4% higher than a year earlier, while adjusted earnings increased 6%. But the sales picture was less impressive. Global comparable sales rose just 1.3%, down from 3.1% for full-year 2025. In the U.S., comparable sales increased only 0.8%, as higher average checks were partly offset by declining guest counts.

The slowdown illustrates why the McDonald's > NEXT plan and Wednesday's announcement matters. McDonald's shares were down roughly 18% this year as of Tuesday's close and traded around $250, close to their 52-week low.

The company sees chicken and beverages as two of its biggest opportunities to gain market share. The chicken market is roughly twice the size of beef globally and growing faster, while beverages represent another growing segment for the restaurant sector.

McDonald's said it is targeting a 1.5 percentage point share gain in both the chicken and beverage categories by 2030, while maintaining its leadership in the beef market as the top seller of fast-food hamburgers.
